nameStory: The summer tanager gets its name from being most visible during the summer months when it migrates north to breed. Unlike some tanagers that flash through during migration, this rosy-red beauty settles in for the whole warm season, making it the quintessential 'summer' member of its family.
description: The summer tanager is a robin-sized songbird with a thick, pale bill built for cracking tough foods. Males are stunning rose-red all over, while females sport warm yellow-green plumage with orangish tones. These medium-sized birds are part of the cardinal family, sharing that group's sturdy build and strong beaks. In New England, they're uncommon visitors, with only 94 recorded sightings.

idTips.label: Male coloration
idTips.description: Adult males are entirely rose-red or brick-red, lacking the black wings and tail that make scarlet tanagers look like they're wearing a tuxedo

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: Thick, pale yellowish bill that looks chunky and seed-cracker-strong, noticeably heavier than most songbird bills

idTips.label: Female appearance
idTips.description: Females are warm yellow-green with orange-yellow tinges, especially on the head and underparts, creating a golden glow

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Robin-sized with a stocky, thick-necked appearance that gives them a more robust look than their scarlet cousins

idTips.label: Voice
idTips.description: Song sounds like a robin with a sore throat - melodic phrases delivered in a hoarser, raspier voice than expected

habitat: In New England, summer tanagers prefer mature deciduous and mixed forests, especially areas with oak trees. They favor forest edges, clearings, and parks where the canopy isn't too dense. Look for them in the middle to upper levels of trees, rarely coming down to ground level.

seasonality.spring: Migrants may appear in late May, with males in their brilliant red breeding plumage leading the way. Listen for their distinctive hoarse robin-like songs in the treetops.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for sightings, as breeding birds settle into territories. Both males and females are active in the canopy, with males singing regularly and both sexes foraging for insects.
seasonality.fall: Birds begin migrating south by August, with juveniles showing mottled red and yellow plumage. Sightings become increasingly rare through September.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England, having migrated to Central and South America for the winter months.

funFact: Summer tanagers are expert bee and wasp hunters, able to catch these stinging insects in mid-air, then beat them against branches to remove the stingers before swallowing them whole - they're like tiny aerial beekeepers!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the scarlet tanager, but remember: summer tanagers are red all over (no black wings), while scarlet tanagers look like they're wearing a black cape and gloves. Think 'summer tanager = solid red superman, scarlet tanager = red bird in a black tuxedo.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called tanagers, summer tanagers were recently moved from the tanager family to the cardinal family based on genetic studies. This explains why their bills look more like a cardinal's than a true tanager's - they're actually more closely related to cardinals and grosbeaks.
compareHints: Summer tanagers are the only all-red Piranga tanager - scarlet tanagers have black wings and tails, while western tanagers show yellow and black markings. Among cardinals and allies, summer tanagers are slimmer than northern cardinals and lack the crest, while being much redder than any grosbeak species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Scarlet tanagers are the only Piranga tanager regularly found in New England, though summer tanagers occasionally wander north.
Western Tanagers are easily distinguished from Scarlet Tanagers by their yellow (not red) bodies and prominent white wing bars.
Hepatic tanagers are much darker red than scarlet tanagers and have pale bills versus dark bills.
